title: Abstinences
hook: right speech, action and livelihood as moments of mind, not just rules

segments.voice: Yesterday, six pairs: calm, lightness, softness, workability, skill and straightness. Your line: soft and workable. Which part of you softened first? Day one thousand eighty.

Dinner with friends, and someone brings up a person who isn't there. A remark is ready on the tongue: a joke that would land, and sting. The mouth is already open, the laugh around the table already half imagined. Then, for whatever reason, it closes again, and someone passes the bread. Nothing happened. Nothing was said. And yet the Abhidhamma says something did happen in that moment, something specific enough to have its own name.

The manual calls it virati, abstinence, and it names three. Right speech: turning away from lies, harsh words, divisive talk and idle chatter. Right action: turning away from killing, stealing and sexual misconduct. Right livelihood: turning away from earning a living in harmful ways. In the suttas these are part of the eightfold path, a way of life. In the Abhidhamma they become something smaller and sharper: a mental factor that arises in the very moment the mind turns away from a wrong it could have done. Not a rule on a wall. A moment. The commentaries tell a story to show it. A young man named Cakkana had a mother who was very sick, and a doctor said fresh hare's meat would cure her. He went to the field and caught a hare. Then, holding it, he thought: it isn't right to take one life to save another, even my mother's. He let it go. Tradition says he came home, solemnly declared that he had never knowingly harmed a living being, and his mother recovered. The commentators use the story for one kind of abstinence: refraining when the chance arrives, with no vow made beforehand. They name two more: refraining because of precepts one has taken, and a last kind that comes with awakening, when the urge is uprooted for good. The Dhammapada gathers the three doors in one verse, in Max Müller's words: "The wise who control their body, who control their tongue, the wise who control their mind, are indeed well controlled." Here is what the Abhidhamma adds. A precept kept for years is made of moments. Each time the hand doesn't take and the tongue doesn't cut, a fresh moment of virati arises. Restraint isn't only something a person has. It's something that happens, the next time a remark is ready.
screen: `SPEECH, ACTION, LIVELIHOOD.` · `NOT A RULE: A MOMENT.` · `CAKKANA LETS THE HARE GO.` · then, large: `RESTRAINT IS SOMETHING THAT HAPPENS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: abstain once, knowingly. Sit, and breathe. Then bring to mind one small thing that might happen today that you'd rather not do: a sharp reply, a bit of gossip, one more scroll, a small fib to smooth things over. Choose just one. Now rehearse the moment it would come, and the turning away. Not a vow. Just the turning, once, here, so it's familiar when it arrives. Notice what turning away is like: a small pause, a hand that stays still, a breath. The bell holds the time.
Abstinences. Virati: the moment the mind turns away from a wrong in speech, action or livelihood. Today's word.
Your line: a moment of restraint. Today, abstain once, knowingly, one remark not made, one thing not taken, and notice the moment as it happens. Day one thousand eighty.

howItsDone: Some lay Buddhists formally take the five precepts at a temple or before a monk, and Abhidhamma students learn the three abstinences of right speech, right action and right livelihood as mental factors that arise when a wrong is refrained from.

original.note: Pali virati: abstinence, the mind turning away from a wrong in the moment.

trapdoor: what you thought: abstinence means giving something up for good.
what it means: a moment when the mind turns away from wrong speech, action or livelihood.
what a scholar hears: the commentaries name three kinds: refraining when the chance comes, refraining by a precept taken, and refraining by uprooting at awakening.

notes: The three abstinences (samma vaca, samma kammanta, samma ajiva) are from Abhidhammattha Sangaha ch. 2; the glosses of each follow the standard sutta definitions (e.g. SN 45.8). Confirm.

Cakkana story: told in the commentaries (Atthasalini; also cited in Bhikkhu Bodhi's guide to the Abhidhammattha Sangaha) as the example of sampatta-virati. Details paraphrased: the doctor's prescription, catching and releasing the hare, the act of truth, the mother's recovery. Whether his brother sent him is left out. Confirm the source and details before release.
The three kinds (sampatta-virati, samadana-virati, samuccheda-virati) are commentarial. Confirm.
'when the urge is uprooted for good' simplifies samuccheda-virati (abstinence by eradication, at path moments).
